evidence_quotes.quote: The aim of this paper is to identify the main gaps, opportunities and priorities for the city of Bandung to address its challenges of water, waste, and climate change.

The 24 indicators of CBF are scored quantitatively mostly using municipal data on a scale from 0 (low performance) to 10 (high performance) and their geometric mean is known as the Blue City Index (BCI) (Koop and van Leeuwen 2020b).

evidence_quotes.page: PMC7891434 - City Blueprint assessment of Bandung's integrated water resources management
evidence_quotes.quote: Bandung's scores for access to sanitation and drinking water are 6.2 and 6.7, respectively, while drinking water quality received a score of 5.9, showing that there is room for improvement.

evidence_quotes.page: PMC7891434 - City Blueprint assessment of Bandung's integrated water resources management
evidence_quotes.quote: The conditions worsen in informal settlements where connection to the central WWTP is nonexistent. Among the slum population in the Greater Bandung Area, only 16.8% collect their wastewater into septic tanks, and 43.4% dispose their wastewater into drainage networks, while 39.6% discharge wastewater directly into rivers (Sofyan et al. 2016).

Bandung's overall governance capacity is clearly limited, as shown by 3 indicators (Table 1). Underperformance is observed for smart monitoring (indicator 3.1), which may limit policy evaluation (indicator 3.2) and results in limited statutory compliance (indicator 9.2).

evidence_quotes.page: PMC7891434 - Transferring the results of Bandung to other cities
evidence_quotes.quote: The main governance challenges are most likely institutional fragmentation, ambiguous legislation, and poor implementation of multilayered governance, as well as matters such as limited capacity at the local level, unclear allocation of roles and responsibilities, fragmented financial management, and uncertain allocation of resources (OECD 2015, 2016; Figure 4).

country.comment: Primary empirical assessment focuses on the city of Bandung, Indonesia (and compares Bandung's results with secondary City Blueprint findings from Jakarta, Indonesia, and other Asian cities).
country.where_found: PMC7891434 - TITLE; INTRODUCTION; Transferring the results of Bandung to other cities

effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive quantitative CBF indicator scores and semiquantitative GCF Likert ratings (-- to ++) for a single city; no statistical regression or causal point estimate is reported.
effect_estimate.value: Bandung scored a Blue City Index (BCI) of 2.6 on a 0–10 scale ('wasteful city'), with City Blueprint Performance Framework (CBF) scores of 6.7 for drinking water access, 6.2 for sanitation access, 5.9 for drinking water quality, and 35% water system leakage / nonrevenue water (synthesized municipal figures show 73% piped water coverage by utility Tirtawening and 35% centralized sewerage connection to Bojongsoang WWTP citywide, versus nonexistent central WWTP connection and 16.8% septic tank use in Greater Bandung slums). On the Governance Capacity Framework (GCF, Likert scale -- to ++, Table 1), Bandung scored 'limiting' (-) across all 5 water challenges for smart monitoring (3.1), policy evaluation (3.2), and statutory compliance (9.2), while scoring 'encouraging' (+) for clear division of responsibilities (7.2) across all 5 challenges and for stakeholder engagement (4.1–4.3) in wastewater treatment; no inferential numeric effect estimate linking legal/governance factors to service access is reported.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 1 (documented descriptive association / co-occurring indicator profile) under the MMAT design ceiling of 2: the study documents Bandung's city-level governance capacity scores (e.g., limiting statutory compliance, monitoring, and evaluation; Table 1) alongside city-level water and sanitation CBF scores (6.7 and 6.2), while specific legal/institutional mechanisms affecting last-mile access (such as 'slum area legalization' cited from Tarigan et al. 2016 and 'institutional fragmentation, ambiguous legislation' cited from OECD 2015, 2016 as 'most likely') are drawn from secondary literature or posited at the macro level rather than directly observed operating on household access.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines slum tenure security and 'slum area legalization' (ELIGIBILITY, tenure), spatial and strategic urban water planning including non-compliance with Indonesia Spatial Planning Act No 26/2007 (planning), administrative 'room to maneuver' and central-government constraints on local officials (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, discretion), stakeholder engagement and participatory community-based sanitation / Kampung Improvement Program (participation), municipal supervision and assistance for community-based sanitation users (bureaucratic_assistance), limited statutory compliance and need to enforce environmental legislation (ENFORCEMENT), and multilevel governance gaps, institutional fragmentation, and central-regional-municipal coordination (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination).

study_design.comment: Applies the 3-part City Blueprint Approach to Bandung, combining quantitative indicator benchmarking from national/municipal secondary data (TPF and CBF) with a semiquantitative Likert-scale water governance diagnostic (GCF) informed by stakeholder input and literature synthesis.
study_design.value: Diagnostic mixed-methods single-city case study applying the City Blueprint Approach (quantitative Trends and Pressures Framework and City Blueprint Performance Framework using secondary national/municipal data, combined with semiquantitative Governance Capacity Framework Likert-scale assessment with stakeholder input and literature synthesis)
